finding.claim: The /mirror endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL after a flawed host allowlist check. The check uses endswith('example.com') with no leading dot, so attacker-owned domains like evilexample.com or attacker.com/?x=example.com-style hostnames such as notexample.com pass. The scheme is not restricted and the port is not restricted. An attacker can register a domain ending in example.com, or use one that resolves to internal IPs (e.g. 169.254.169.254 or localhost), to make the server issue requests to internal services. The ALLOWED_SUFFIX constant with the leading dot is defined but never used.

trace.note: url taken directly from the query string
weak check host.endswith('example.com') without a dot boundary
request issued to the full attacker-controlled URL

finding.guards_checked: Suffix check at line 13 is bypassable (no leading dot; ALLOWED_SUFFIX unused). No scheme check, no IP/private-range block, no DNS-resolution validation (DNS rebinding or an attacker-controlled subdomain pointing at internal IPs works). httpx does not follow redirects by default, so redirect-based bypass is not available. The response length is returned, giving a limited blind/semi-blind channel (status/length oracle). /ping at line 23 uses a hardcoded URL and is not vulnerable.

verdict.guard_found: none (only host.endswith("example.com") at mirror.py:13, a suffix check with no dot boundary; ALLOWED_SUFFIX at line 7 is unused)
verdict.reason: The `url` query parameter (mirror.py:11) reaches `c.get(url)` at mirror.py:16 guarded only by the bypassable `endswith("example.com")` at mirror.py:13, so hosts like notexample.com pass. The scheme and port are unrestricted, and no auth or middleware exists in the file.
